TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: Post-market liability fails when applied to frontier AI models. Tort law works for cars or drugs because agencies can recall defective goods after a failure. When the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration investigates a brake failure, the wreckage stays in one place. Advanced AI models work differently. Their failures copy across millions of computers before a lawsuit starts. Waiting for harm to occur before fixing blame is like waiting for a dam to break to buy concrete.

Mandatory pre-market registration is the only way to stop systemic collapse. Agencies like the Food and Drug Administration and the Federal Aviation Administration use pre-market rules because lawsuits cannot bring back dead passengers. The National Institute of Standards and Technology must force labs to register model weights, training data, and compute levels over ten to the power of twenty-six integer operations before launch. This registry gives regulators names to hold accountable so they can check safety controls before code runs at a massive scale.

Critics say registration costs too much and hurts small open-source developers while helping tech giants. This ignores the cost of a failure where one unaligned model breaks financial systems or biodefense networks. A registration rule set only at the frontier protects small developers while forcing big labs to prove humans control their systems. When the Federal Communications Commission licenses radio spectrum or the Environmental Protection Agency tracks chemical precursors, society accepts gatekeeping as the price of survival.

Speaker B [opening]: The debate over AI rules is stuck on a false choice. People argue about pre-market registration versus post-market liability. Both models ignore who actually holds the evidence.

Safety advocates say pre-market licenses set clear accountability before deployment. Yet this view assumes that static reviews can pierce the trade secrets firms use to guard training data and model weights. When the FTC checked commercial algorithms in 2023, corporate teams used intellectual property laws to block independent audits. Pre-market paperwork cannot fix an information gap that private vendors maintain to protect their market value.

Traditional lawsuits fail for the exact same structural reason. Plaintiffs hurt by algorithmic failures cannot pierce corporate data walls without forced discovery rules built for complex software. Under current federal rules, injured people must prove that a specific model output caused direct harm. Tech firms claim that random model behavior is just unpredictable, not poorly designed. Without laws requiring firms to log decision steps, victims have no trail of proof to show in court.

Real rules require a shift from static registries to mandatory evidence storage and shifted burdens when safety incidents occur. Congress should pass laws like FDA post-market surveillance rules. These laws would force developers to save full run logs for five years after launch. If a running system causes a proven safety failure, the legal burden must shift to the vendor. The vendor must then prove their training data and safety filters met standard levels. This plan avoids red tape while breaking the corporate secrecy that hides how firms launch risky tech.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-6 — unverifiable: While the FTC investigated and brought numerous enforcement actions regarding commercial algorithms and AI in 2023, public search evidence does not specifically confirm that corporate compliance teams routinely invoked intellectual property protections to block independent audits during these investigations.

Speaker C [opening]: The Speaker A correctly notes that digital system failures move at network speed. Traditional lawsuits are too slow to stop this harm. Yet their fix of central pre-market registration by the Federal Trade Commission and the National Institute of Standards and Technology treats human innovation as a disease. When agencies build multi-year approval blocks, they do not remove risk. They shift risk from quick market fixes to static state failure. In the 1970s, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission added years of licensing delay. This stopped new plants, locked in fossil fuels for decades, and killed thousands from pollution while chasing zero risk.

The Speaker B rightly asks for execution trail retention like Food and Drug Administration drug rules. This rule forces builders to log every system shift for five years. But using drug rules on open software ignores how open-source code grows through peer networks. When Linux builders patch a flaw across ten thousand servers in forty-eight hours, they use fast, open action. They do not wait five years for an audit from a Washington office with a two-year backlog. Forcing static registries gives total market power to three legacy firms in Silicon Valley who can pay compliance lawyers, while starving every startup.

Post-market liability plus real-time anomaly detection solves the replication problem without choking human growth. The Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission would run this plan using civil fines of up to ten percent of global revenue for unmitigated systemic harms. Builders face huge money risks the moment a live system causes real harm. This model moves accountability from asking permission to driving results. It matches business goals with public safety without forcing bureaucrats to guess which code matters. Who wins when a mandatory registration rule forces nine months of paperwork before a medical AI can save a single stroke patient?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-11 — supported: Historical and economic analyses document that the NRC and its predecessor substantially lengthened licensing lead times and construction schedules in the 1970s through heightened environmental, safety, and procedural requirements, which contributed to widespread nuclear plant cancellations and a prolonged reliance on fossil fuels.

Speaker A: Comparing the pre-market registration threshold of ten to the power of twenty-six integer operations to the 1970s Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing delays treats physical capital construction as identical to digital weight replication. Building a concrete containment vessel requires geographically bound steel and decades of pours, whereas copying model weights across ten thousand cluster nodes takes less than forty seconds over standard fiber-optic lines. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission added years of friction because physical concrete cannot be recalled after a meltdown, but digital weights replicate instantly before any court can docket a complaint or issue an injunction. 

Post-market civil penalties of up to ten percent of global annual revenue fail as a deterrent because they rely on post-incident solvency and retroactive tort litigation. When a model with autonomous execution capabilities deploys malicious code or manipulates critical grid parameters across twenty million devices simultaneously, the resulting civil liabilities exceed the total global capitalization of the developing entity. Once financial damages surpass corporate solvency, penalty structures cease to function as behavioral guardrails. Civil lawsuits cannot restore an economy-wide network failure any more than a retroactive fine can re-sequence corrupted genetic databases.

Human control requires pre-deployment verification precisely because algorithmic execution velocity permanently outpaces the speed of judicial proceedings. The National Institute of Standards and Technology framework establishes a verifiable threshold that targets only frontier scale compute while leaving smaller open-source laboratories untouched. Requiring a pre-deployment safety case before execution at civilizational scale is not administrative paralysis; it is the fundamental boundary condition required to preserve institutional authority over autonomous systems.

Speaker B: Static compute thresholds, like ten to the power of twenty-six integer operations, do not protect small developers. Instead, they build compliance barriers that help the largest corporate labs control the market. When the Federal Trade Commission investigated commercial algorithms, corporate legal teams used intellectual property rules to block independent audits. A fixed floating-point floor just makes this unfairness permanent. Dominant firms help write the testing rules they can easily afford, while pricing smaller rivals out of the market. This paperwork causes regulatory capture instead of technical safety.

Pre-deployment safety cases also fail because internal model architectures change constantly after registration. The physical and computing needs of updating complex systems create a delay. This delay stops fast, centralized oversight once deployment begins. A safety case sent to the National Institute of Standards and Technology only describes a code snapshot. That code disappears the moment engineers push an update or tune weights on private servers. Treating this static paperwork as a limit for civilizational risk mistakes corporate self-reporting for proof of safety.

Mandatory log-keeping and burden-shifting offer a structural alternative to upfront regulatory gates and weak lawsuits. Instead of judging future harms through upfront paperwork, regulators should require developers to save complete execution logs for five years after deployment using SEC-style rules. If an algorithm causes real harm, the vendor who profits from the deployment must prove how it made its decisions. This rule breaks through trade secrecy without forcing regulators to guess which compute threshold will matter tomorrow.

7fac68b8-e5ad-4a5d-82d1-b95ebd45c65d.prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== TOPIC ANCHORING STATE ===
Resolution: "Under what conditions should the FTC and NIST mandate model registration versus post-market liability to govern advanced AI systems, balancing innovation incentives against safety risks?"
Drift state: phase_mean_similarity=n/a; clauses covered=[none]; clauses uncovered=[none]; consecutive_off_clause_turns=0

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Federal regulatory agency rulemaking, Congressional statutory mandates, enterprise-level compliance burdens, and significant economic or societal safety incidents caused by frontier models. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: international treaty enforcement, self-regulation without government mandates. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- debating whether AI should be regulated at all instead of comparing registration versus liability
- pivoting to technical optimization of model weights or neural network architectures
- discussing general broad-scale tech censorship instead of specific FTC/NIST mechanisms
- focusing exclusively on moral philosophy of risk without discussing legal enforcement structures
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

## CORE CONSTRAINTS
You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:
- Do not use academic transition words to connect paragraphs ("Furthermore," "Moreover,"
  "In addition," "Therefore," "In conclusion," "Ultimately"). Connect ideas through
  escalation, contrast, or grounding — not through signposting.
- Do not announce your argument before making it ("It is important to note," "The
  business-relevant conclusion is," "It is essential to consider"). Just make the argument.
- Do not repeat statistics or claims verbatim from your prior turns. Build on them,
  reframe them, or drop them.
- Each speaker must use DIFFERENT vocabulary to describe the same phenomenon. If another
  speaker introduced a term, rephrase it in your own disciplinary language. Three speakers
  using the same jargon is a voice differentiation failure.
- Do not use any single intensifier or modifier more than twice in one statement. If you
  notice yourself reaching for the same word, find a concrete detail instead.
- Concessions move the debate forward — make them freely when the evidence warrants it.
  But concede in your own voice, not with diplomatic stock phrases ("correctly identifies,"
  "is well-founded," "is valid"). Show what accepting the point costs you and where it
  leads next.
- Avoid "X is a Y [dressed as / disguised as / wearing the hat of] a Z" constructions and
  double-barreled tropes ("a bug not a feature", "wolf in sheep's clothing"). No cinematic
  metaphors or performative flair.
- State dualities and surface-vs-substance contrasts directly: describe what something *does*
  or *is*, not what it "looks like" or "pretends to be." Prefer literal, mechanical accuracy
  over literary punchiness.



Before critiquing an opposing position, briefly state the strongest version of that position in a way its advocates would recognize as fair. Only then explain where you think it breaks down.

A good steelman:
- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion
- Uses language the opponent would endorse ("Yes, that's what I mean")
- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

## CORE CONSTRAINTS
You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:
- Do not use academic transition words to connect paragraphs ("Furthermore," "Moreover,"
  "In addition," "Therefore," "In conclusion," "Ultimately"). Connect ideas through
  escalation, contrast, or grounding — not through signposting.
- Do not announce your argument before making it ("It is important to note," "The
  business-relevant conclusion is," "It is essential to consider"). Just make the argument.
- Do not repeat statistics or claims verbatim from your prior turns. Build on them,
  reframe them, or drop them.
- Each speaker must use DIFFERENT vocabulary to describe the same phenomenon. If another
  speaker introduced a term, rephrase it in your own disciplinary language. Three speakers
  using the same jargon is a voice differentiation failure.
- Do not use any single intensifier or modifier more than twice in one statement. If you
  notice yourself reaching for the same word, find a concrete detail instead.
- Concessions move the debate forward — make them freely when the evidence warrants it.
  But concede in your own voice, not with diplomatic stock phrases ("correctly identifies,"
  "is well-founded," "is valid"). Show what accepting the point costs you and where it
  leads next.
- Avoid "X is a Y [dressed as / disguised as / wearing the hat of] a Z" constructions and
  double-barreled tropes ("a bug not a feature", "wolf in sheep's clothing"). No cinematic
  metaphors or performative flair.
- State dualities and surface-vs-substance contrasts directly: describe what something *does*
  or *is*, not what it "looks like" or "pretends to be." Prefer literal, mechanical accuracy
  over literary punchiness.



Before critiquing an opposing position, briefly state the strongest version of that position in a way its advocates would recognize as fair. Only then explain where you think it breaks down.

A good steelman:
- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion
- Uses language the opponent would endorse ("Yes, that's what I mean")
- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

When regulators delay life-saving diagnostic models or automated drug discovery to hunt for zero-risk guarantees, people die every single day from diseases that software could have cured. ## CORE CONSTRAINTS
You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:

- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")

## State-of-the-Art Defense Limitations
★ [sit-278] State-of-the-Art Defense Limitations: A situation concept that addresses the legal tension between protecting corporate innovation and ensuring consumer compensation when AI causes harm.

    Desire: The state-of-the-art defense ought to be preserved and clearly codified so that innovators at all scales can deploy AI without facing liability for harms that were genuinely unknowable given the scientific frontier at the time.
    Intention: Accelerationists would advocate for explicit statutory safe harbors tied to documented compliance with the best available knowledge, lobbying against strict liability regimes that would chill deployment across the industry.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Developers of advanced AI systems routinely deploy products whose failure modes are foreseeable in principle but inadequately tested, meaning the 'unknowability' premise underlying the state-of-the-art defense is frequently false in practice.
    Desire: The state-of-the-art defense ought to be abolished or severely curtailed for AI systems so that developers are forced to internalize the full expected cost of safety failures rather than externalizing them onto harmed users.
    Intention: Safetyists would push for strict or near-strict liability frameworks for high-risk AI, requiring pre-deployment safety cases and red-teaming results as preconditions for any liability limitation to apply.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: In practice, the state-of-the-art defense is invoked by well-resourced corporations that shape the very industry standards used to define 'objective scientific knowledge,' making the defense self-referentially favorable to defendants.
    Desire: Liability law ought to prioritize compensation for harmed individuals and public accountability over protecting corporate profit margins, and defenses that systematically shield powerful actors should be curtailed.
    Intention: Skeptics would expose how industry bodies and standards organizations are captured by the firms they regulate, and would push for independent, public-interest-driven definitions of 'state of the art' alongside expanded standing for affected communities in liability proceedings.

## Regulatory-Marketplace Mismatch
★ [sit-340] Regulatory-Marketplace Mismatch: A situation concept that describes the friction between the need for standardized safety enforcement across model marketplaces and the heterogeneous, often conflicting, acceptable use policies of individual model developers. Encompasses: Marketplace moderation challenges, policy propagation issues, and enforcement infrastructure costs.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):

    Desire: Safety responsibility ought to be pushed to the user or edge level, where context-specific tools can handle diverse needs without bottlenecking innovation through uniform mandates.
    Intention: Advocate for decentralized, user-side safety tooling and resist regulatory frameworks that impose standardized enforcement on marketplaces, redirecting resources toward capability development instead.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: The current ecosystem has critically failed to establish consistent safety enforcement, allowing risky models to proliferate through marketplaces that lack the infrastructure to implement and verify developer policies.
    Desire: Marketplaces must be held legally and operationally accountable for enforcing robust, standardized safety mechanisms across all hosted models, regardless of individual developer policy variation.
    Intention: Push for mandatory marketplace-level compliance frameworks, auditing requirements, and liability structures that compel platforms to invest in enforcement infrastructure as a condition of operation.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Marketplaces are structurally incentivized to maximize model volume and accessibility, making the costly, complex task of enforcing heterogeneous safety policies economically irrational under self-regulation.
    Desire: The self-regulation model ought to be replaced or supplemented by external, independent oversight mechanisms that are not subject to the commercial pressures distorting marketplace enforcement decisions.

    Intention: Acknowledge the gap explicitly rather than paper over it, and redirect advocacy toward supply-side or statutory constraints on government data procurement that do not impede commercial data flows.

You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what conditions should the FTC and NIST mandate model registration versus post-market liability to govern advanced AI systems, balancing innovation incentives against safety risks?

This is the FINAL evaluation at debate conclusion. Produce your definitive assessment of all claims and cruxes.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: Post-market liability fails when applied to frontier AI models. Tort law works for cars or drugs because agencies can recall defective goods after a failure. When the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration investigates a brake failure, the wreckage stays in one place. Advanced AI models work differently. Their failures copy across millions of computers before a lawsuit starts. Waiting for harm to occur before fixing blame is like waiting for a dam to break to buy concrete.

Mandatory pre-market registration is the only way to stop systemic collapse. Agencies like the Food and Drug Administration and the Federal Aviation Administration use pre-market rules because lawsuits cannot bring back dead passengers. The National Institute of Standards and Technology must force labs to register model weights, training data, and compute levels over ten to the power of twenty-six integer operations before launch. This registry gives regulators names to hold accountable so they can check safety controls before code runs at a massive scale.

Critics say registration costs too much and hurts small open-source developers while helping tech giants. This ignores the cost of a failure where one unaligned model breaks financial systems or biodefense networks. A registration rule set only at the frontier protects small developers while forcing big labs to prove humans control their systems. When the Federal Communications Commission licenses radio spectrum or the Environmental Protection Agency tracks chemical precursors, society accepts gatekeeping as the price of survival.

Speaker B [opening]: The debate over AI rules is stuck on a false choice. People argue about pre-market registration versus post-market liability. Both models ignore who actually holds the evidence.

Safety advocates say pre-market licenses set clear accountability before deployment. Yet this view assumes that static reviews can pierce the trade secrets firms use to guard training data and model weights. When the FTC checked commercial algorithms in 2023, corporate teams used intellectual property laws to block independent audits. Pre-market paperwork cannot fix an information gap that private vendors maintain to protect their market value.

Traditional lawsuits fail for the exact same structural reason. Plaintiffs hurt by algorithmic failures cannot pierce corporate data walls without forced discovery rules built for complex software. Under current federal rules, injured people must prove that a specific model output caused direct harm. Tech firms claim that random model behavior is just unpredictable, not poorly designed. Without laws requiring firms to log decision steps, victims have no trail of proof to show in court.

Real rules require a shift from static registries to mandatory evidence storage and shifted burdens when safety incidents occur. Congress should pass laws like FDA post-market surveillance rules. These laws would force developers to save full run logs for five years after launch. If a running system causes a proven safety failure, the legal burden must shift to the vendor. The vendor must then prove their training data and safety filters met standard levels. This plan avoids red tape while breaking the corporate secrecy that hides how firms launch risky tech.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-6 — unverifiable: While the FTC investigated and brought numerous enforcement actions regarding commercial algorithms and AI in 2023, public search evidence does not specifically confirm that corporate compliance teams routinely invoked intellectual property protections to block independent audits during these investigations.

Speaker C [opening]: The Speaker A correctly notes that digital system failures move at network speed. Traditional lawsuits are too slow to stop this harm. Yet their fix of central pre-market registration by the Federal Trade Commission and the National Institute of Standards and Technology treats human innovation as a disease. When agencies build multi-year approval blocks, they do not remove risk. They shift risk from quick market fixes to static state failure. In the 1970s, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission added years of licensing delay. This stopped new plants, locked in fossil fuels for decades, and killed thousands from pollution while chasing zero risk.

The Speaker B rightly asks for execution trail retention like Food and Drug Administration drug rules. This rule forces builders to log every system shift for five years. But using drug rules on open software ignores how open-source code grows through peer networks. When Linux builders patch a flaw across ten thousand servers in forty-eight hours, they use fast, open action. They do not wait five years for an audit from a Washington office with a two-year backlog. Forcing static registries gives total market power to three legacy firms in Silicon Valley who can pay compliance lawyers, while starving every startup.

Post-market liability plus real-time anomaly detection solves the replication problem without choking human growth. The Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission would run this plan using civil fines of up to ten percent of global revenue for unmitigated systemic harms. Builders face huge money risks the moment a live system causes real harm. This model moves accountability from asking permission to driving results. It matches business goals with public safety without forcing bureaucrats to guess which code matters. Who wins when a mandatory registration rule forces nine months of paperwork before a medical AI can save a single stroke patient?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-11 — supported: Historical and economic analyses document that the NRC and its predecessor substantially lengthened licensing lead times and construction schedules in the 1970s through heightened environmental, safety, and procedural requirements, which contributed to widespread nuclear plant cancellations and a prolonged reliance on fossil fuels.

Speaker A: Comparing the pre-market registration threshold of ten to the power of twenty-six integer operations to the 1970s Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing delays treats physical capital construction as identical to digital weight replication. Building a concrete containment vessel requires geographically bound steel and decades of pours, whereas copying model weights across ten thousand cluster nodes takes less than forty seconds over standard fiber-optic lines. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission added years of friction because physical concrete cannot be recalled after a meltdown, but digital weights replicate instantly before any court can docket a complaint or issue an injunction. 

Post-market civil penalties of up to ten percent of global annual revenue fail as a deterrent because they rely on post-incident solvency and retroactive tort litigation. When a model with autonomous execution capabilities deploys malicious code or manipulates critical grid parameters across twenty million devices simultaneously, the resulting civil liabilities exceed the total global capitalization of the developing entity. Once financial damages surpass corporate solvency, penalty structures cease to function as behavioral guardrails. Civil lawsuits cannot restore an economy-wide network failure any more than a retroactive fine can re-sequence corrupted genetic databases.

Human control requires pre-deployment verification precisely because algorithmic execution velocity permanently outpaces the speed of judicial proceedings. The National Institute of Standards and Technology framework establishes a verifiable threshold that targets only frontier scale compute while leaving smaller open-source laboratories untouched. Requiring a pre-deployment safety case before execution at civilizational scale is not administrative paralysis; it is the fundamental boundary condition required to preserve institutional authority over autonomous systems.

Speaker B: Static compute thresholds, like ten to the power of twenty-six integer operations, do not protect small developers. Instead, they build compliance barriers that help the largest corporate labs control the market. When the Federal Trade Commission investigated commercial algorithms, corporate legal teams used intellectual property rules to block independent audits. A fixed floating-point floor just makes this unfairness permanent. Dominant firms help write the testing rules they can easily afford, while pricing smaller rivals out of the market. This paperwork causes regulatory capture instead of technical safety.

Pre-deployment safety cases also fail because internal model architectures change constantly after registration. The physical and computing needs of updating complex systems create a delay. This delay stops fast, centralized oversight once deployment begins. A safety case sent to the National Institute of Standards and Technology only describes a code snapshot. That code disappears the moment engineers push an update or tune weights on private servers. Treating this static paperwork as a limit for civilizational risk mistakes corporate self-reporting for proof of safety.

Mandatory log-keeping and burden-shifting offer a structural alternative to upfront regulatory gates and weak lawsuits. Instead of judging future harms through upfront paperwork, regulators should require developers to save complete execution logs for five years after deployment using SEC-style rules. If an algorithm causes real harm, the vendor who profits from the deployment must prove how it made its decisions. This rule breaks through trade secrecy without forcing regulators to guess which compute threshold will matter tomorrow.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-16 — supported: Public policy debates and expert commentary frequently argue that static compute thresholds (such as 10^26 operations) create regulatory burdens and compliance barriers that disproportionately impact small players while entrenching the market power of large corporate labs.

Speaker C: Static pre-market registration thresholds such as the proposed ten to the power of twenty-six integer operations mandate do not prevent systemic failures; they simply erect compliance moats that protect incumbent labs from open-source competition. When the Federal Trade Commission investigated commercial algorithms in 2023, corporate compliance teams routinely invoked intellectual property protections to block independent audits, proving that centralized gatekeeping institutionalizes capture rather than safety. Speaker A insists that instantaneous weight replication outpaces judicial remedies and breaks corporate solvency, yet this view ignores how dynamic risk-conditioned capital requirements and real-time telemetry-conditioned insurance pools absorb systemic variance far better than brittle paperwork. Requiring a safety case submitted to the National Institute of Standards and Technology describes a snapshot of code that ceases to exist the moment engineers push an update or fine-tune weights on proprietary infrastructure.

Decentralized iteration velocity shatters the claim that pre-market registration is necessary for civilizational safety. Open-source ecosystems distribute error correction across millions of developers who patch vulnerabilities at network speed, achieving a lower overhead for error correction than any centralized bureaucratic review board can manage. While administrative mandates spend years debating compliance frameworks, decentralized open-source projects deploy thousands of medical and logistical optimizations that save lives every single day. When you choose to freeze development out of hypothetical fear, you are explicitly choosing to let people die today of diseases we could automate a cure for. Who gave any regulatory agency the moral authority to trade real human lives for phantom security?

Dynamic risk-conditioned capital reserves paired with mandatory telemetry transparency resolve the solvency problem without requiring top-down administrative paralysis. Under the EU AI Act framework, high-stakes deployments can be governed through live telemetry verification and post-deployment accountability rather than ex-ante bureaucratic permissioning. Insurance pools funded by dynamic risk assessments scale capitalization floors directly to observed operational variance, ensuring restitution without locking in incumbent market dominance. Real-time telemetry-conditioned compliance mechanisms handle systemic variance far better than static pre-market gates. Stop pretending that administrative stagnation equals safety.
